passages.happening:
Naomi speaks to Ruth. “My daughter, should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?” (verse 1). Boaz, whose young women Ruth has worked beside, is their relative, and tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor (verse 2).

So Naomi tells her to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, and go down to the threshing floor. She is not to let Boaz know she is there until he has finished eating and drinking. When he lies down, she is to note the place, go in, uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell her what to do (verses 3-4).

“I will do everything you say,” Ruth answered (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A ‘resting place’ means settled security: a home and a husband. On the road in chapter 1, Naomi had prayed that her daughters-in-law would find rest in a husband's house. Now she sets out to find it for Ruth herself.

Threshing and winnowing were done on a flat, hard open space, often on high ground where the wind was steady. The stalks were beaten to loosen the grain, and then the mixture was tossed into the air so that the evening breeze carried off the chaff and the heavier grain fell back. The harvested grain was valuable, so owners and workers slept beside the heap to guard it. That is why Boaz will be there at night.

Washing, perfume and her best clothes may mark the end of Ruth's time of mourning as a widow.

Naomi's plan is bold and risky. It puts a young foreign widow alone at night near a man who has been eating and drinking. Everything depends on the kind of man Boaz is.
passages.later:
Naomi's word for rest is the word of her prayer on the road: “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband” (Ruth 1:9).

Another widow in Judah's family took a bold step to claim her right, and the notes on Genesis 38 set the two side by side: Tamar with Judah, and Ruth with Boaz. Ruth is honorable where Judah was not, and Boaz acts rightly where Judah did not (Genesis 38:14).
passages.asks: Naomi stopped looking only at her own grief and began to plan for Ruth's future. Ask whose future you could care for, even while you are still carrying your own loss. And ask what risks love has asked of you, and whether you have trusted God with them.

passages.happening:
Ruth goes down and does all that Naomi told her (verse 6). Boaz eats and drinks, is in good spirits, and lies down at the end of the heap of grain. Ruth comes quietly, uncovers his feet and lies down (verse 7).

At midnight Boaz wakes with a start, turns over, and there is a woman lying at his feet (verse 8). “Who are you?” he asked. “I am your servant Ruth,” she replied. “Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer” (verse 9).

Boaz answers, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter.” Her kindness now is greater than before, because she has not gone after younger men, rich or poor (verse 10). He tells her not to be afraid. He will do all she asks, for everyone in town knows she is ‘a woman of noble character’ (verse 11). But there is a redeemer nearer than he. In the morning, if that man will redeem her, good. If not, “as surely as the LORD lives, I will” (verses 12-13).

She lies at his feet until morning and gets up before anyone could recognize her, and Boaz says that no one must know a woman came to the threshing floor (verse 14). He pours six measures of barley into her shawl, and she goes back to the town (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Ruth's request is the heart of the book. To spread the corner of a garment over a woman was a way of taking her in marriage and under protection. The Hebrew word for the corner of a garment also means a wing. In chapter 2 Boaz prayed that the LORD would reward Ruth, ‘under whose wings you have taken refuge’. Now Ruth asks Boaz to spread his wing over her. She is asking him to be the answer to his own prayer.

She also names him a kinsman-redeemer. Under the law, the redeemer bought back land and helped a family in trouble. Marrying a dead man's widow to carry on his name was a separate custom, and strictly it belonged to a brother. Ruth joins the two, asking Boaz to redeem the family by marrying her. Boaz takes the request as an honor, not a presumption.

His praise of her kindness explains why. She could have looked for a younger husband of her own choosing. Instead she has sought a redeemer who can carry on her dead husband's family and care for Naomi.

‘A woman of noble character’ uses the same Hebrew word as the description of Boaz in chapter 2. The two are matched.

He keeps her good name safe, and he sends her home with barley. The narrator keeps the scene discreet, and the hard question below sets out how readers have read it.
passages.later:
God himself uses the picture of spreading a garment's corner when he speaks of taking Israel as his own: “So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness” (Ezekiel 16:8).

The book of Proverbs closes with a poem in praise of ‘A wife of noble character’ (Proverbs 31:10), the same phrase Boaz uses of Ruth.
passages.hard:
What happened at the threshing floor? Was Naomi's plan improper?

The difficulty is real. In Hebrew the words for uncovering, for feet, and for lying down can carry sexual overtones, and the word for feet is sometimes used as a polite substitute elsewhere. So some readers think the scene holds at least a suggestion of seduction, and that the narrator leaves it unclear on purpose.

Most readers, ancient and modern, read it another way. Ruth's act is a bold but chaste proposal. Uncovering Boaz's feet was a way of waking him and making her request without speaking in front of others. They point to the narrator's stress on Ruth's noble character, to Boaz's care for her reputation, and to his refusal to act until the nearer redeemer has been asked. On this reading nothing improper happened.

Both readings agree on the main things. The scene is charged and risky. Ruth put her reputation in Boaz's hands, and Boaz answered with honor and not with advantage. The book's point is his integrity and her loyalty, not the details of the night.
passages.asks: Ruth put her whole future into a single request, and Boaz could have used the moment for himself. Ask how you treat a person who has made themselves vulnerable to you. And ask whether you keep your promises as quickly as Boaz meant to keep his.

passages.happening:
Ruth comes back to her mother-in-law, and Naomi asks how it went. Ruth tells her everything Boaz did (verse 16). “He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed’” (verse 17).

“Wait, my daughter,” said Naomi, “until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is framed by two talks between Naomi and Ruth, one before the night and one after.

‘Empty-handed’ is the same Hebrew word Naomi used in chapter 1: ‘the LORD has brought me back empty’. Boaz's gift answers her complaint. The barley in Ruth's shawl is a sign that the emptiness is being filled.

Naomi, who planned so boldly, now counsels patience. She knows the man. He will not rest until the matter is settled. Ruth has done her part. Now someone else must act.
passages.later: The psalms speak of the same waiting: “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD” (Psalm 27:14).
passages.asks: Ruth had done all she could, and Naomi told her to wait. Ask what you have done all you can about, and whether you can wait without forcing the next step. And think of the barley. Ask what small sign of God's care you have been given in a season of waiting.
